source_text: Ὁρᾷς τὴν ἀκαθαρσίαν οὐκ ἀπὸ τῆς τοῦ πράγματος φύσεως, ἀλλ' ἀπὸ τῆς ἀσθενείας τοῦ λογισμοῦ γινομένην; Καὶ πάλιν, Πάντα μὲν καθαρὰ, ἀλλὰ κακὸν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τῷ διὰ προσκόμματος ἐσθίοντι. Ὁρᾷς ὅτι οὐ τὸ ἐσθίειν, ἀλλὰ τὸ διὰ προσκόμματος ἐσθίειν. τοῦτο αἴτιον ἀκαθαρσίας; γʹ. Τὴν τοιαύτην κηλῖδα τὸ Ἰουδαϊκὸν ἐξεκάθαρε λουτρόν· τὸ δὲ τῆς χάριτος οὐ τοιαύτην, ἀλλὰ τὴν ὄντως ἀκαθαρσίαν τὴν μετὰ τοῦ σώματος καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ πολλὴν ἐντεθεῖσαν τὴν κηλῖδα· οὐ γὰρ τοὺς νεκρῶν ἁψαμένους σωμάτων, ἀλλὰ τοὺς νεκρῶν πράξεων ἁψαμένους τούτους ποιεῖ καθαρούς. Κἂν μαλακὸς, κἂν πόρνος ᾖ τις, κἂν εἰδωλολάτρης, κἂν ὁτιοῦν εἰργασμένος δεινὸν, κἂν ἅπασαν τὴν ἐν ἀνθρώποις πονηρίαν ἔχων ᾖ, ἐμπεσὼν εἰς τὴν τῶν ὑδάτων κολυμβήθραν, τῶν ἡλιακῶν καθαρώτερος ἀκτίνων ἄνεισιν ἀπὸ τῶν θείων ναμάτων. Καὶ ἵνα μὴ νομίσῃς κόμπον εἶναι τὰ λεγόμενα, ἄκουσον Παύλου λέγοντος περὶ τῆς τοῦ λουτροῦ δυνάμεως· Μὴ πλανᾶσθε· οὔτε εἰδωλολάτραι, οὔτε πόρνοι, οὔτε μοιχοὶ, οὔτε μαλακοὶ, οὔτε ἀρσενοκοῖται, οὔτε πλεονέκται, οὐ μέθυσοι, οὐ λοίδοροι, οὐχ ἅρπαγες βασιλείαν Θεοῦ οὐ κληρονομήσουσι. Καὶ τί τοῦτο πρὸς τὰ εἰρημένα, φησί; τὸ γὰρ ζητούμενον δεῖξαι, εἰ πάντα ἐκκαθαίρει ταῦτα ἡ τοῦ λουτροῦ δύναμις. Οὐκοῦν ἄκουσον τῶν ἑξῆς· Καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε, ἀλλ' ἀπελούσασθε, ἀλλ' ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλ' ἐδικαιώθητε ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἐν τῷ Πνεύματι τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν. Ἡμεῖς μὲν ὑπισχνούμεθα δεῖξαι ὑμῖν, καθαροὺς πορνείας γινομένους ἁπάσης τοὺς τῷ λουτρῷ προσιόντας· ὁ δὲ λόγος πλέον ἀπέδειξεν, οὐ καθαροὺς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἁγίους καὶ δικαίους γενομένους· οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν, Ἀπελούσασθε, μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ, Ἡγιάσθητε καὶ ἐδικαιώθητε. Τί τούτου γένοιτ' ἂν παραδοξότερον, ὅταν πόνων καὶ ἱδρώτων χωρὶς καὶ κατορθωμάτων δικαιοσύνη τικτομένη ᾖ; τοιαύτη γὰρ τῆς θείας δωρεᾶς ἡ φιλανθρωπία χωρὶς ἱδρώτων ποιεῖ δικαίους. Εἰ γὰρ βασιλέως ἐπιστολὴ, γράμματα προτεθέντα ὀλίγα, μυρίων ὑπευθύνους ἐγκλημάτων ἀφίησιν ἐλευθέρους, ἑτέρους δὲ καὶ πρὸς τιμὴν ἄγει μεγίστην, πολλῷ μᾶλλον τὸ ἅγιον τοῦ Θεοῦ Πνεῦμα καὶ πάντα δυνάμενον, πάσης μὲν ἡμᾶς ἀπαλλάξει κακίας, πολλὴν δὲ ἡμῖν χαριεῖται δικαιοσύνην, καὶ πολλῆς ἐμπλήσει τῆς παῤῥησίας. Καὶ καθάπερ σπινθὴρ μέσον εἰς πέλαγος ἀχανὲς ἐμπεσὼν εὐθέως ἂν ἀποσβεσθείη, ἢ καὶ ἀφανὴς γένοιτο, τῷ πλήθει τῶν ὑδάτων καταποντισθείς· οὕτω καὶ πᾶσα πονηρία ἀνθρωπίνη, ὅταν εἰς τὴν κολυμβήθραν ἐμπέσῃ τῶν θείων ναμάτων, ἐκείνου ταχύτερον καὶ εὐκολώτερον τοῦ σπινθῆρος καταποντίζεται καὶ ἀφανίζεται. Καὶ τίνος ἕνεκεν, φησὶν, εἰ τὰ ἁμαρτήματα ἡμῖν ἅπαντα ἀφίησι τὸ λουτρὸν, οὐχὶ λουτρὸν ἀφέσεως ἁμαρτημάτων καλεῖται, οὔτε λουτρὸν καθάρσεως, ἀλλὰ λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας; Ὅτι οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἡμῖν ἀφίησι τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, οὐδὲ ἁπλῶς ἡμᾶς καθαίρει τῶν πλημμελημάτων, ἀλλ' οὕτως ὡς ἂν εἰ ἄνωθεν ἐγεννήθημεν. Καὶ γὰρ ἄνωθεν ἡμᾶς δημιουργεῖ καὶ κατασκευάζει, οὐκ ἀπὸ γῆς διαπλάττον πάλιν, ἀλλ' ἐξ ἑτέρου στοιχείου τῆς τῶν ὑδάτων φύσεως δημιουργοῦν. Οὐ γὰρ ἁπλῶς ἀποσμήχει τὸ σκεῦος, ἀλλ' ὁλόκληρον αὐτὸ ἀναχωνεύει πάλιν. Τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἀποσμηχόμενα, κἂν μετὰ ἀκριβείας ἐκκαθαίρηται, ἔχει τῆς ποιότητος ἴχνη καὶ τῆς κηλῖδος φέρει τὰ λείψανα· τὰ δὲ εἰς χωνευτήριον ἐμπεσόντα καὶ διὰ τῆς φλογὸς ἀνανεωθέντα, πᾶσαν ἀποθέμενα ῥυπαρίαν, τὴν αὐτὴν τοῖς νεοπαγέσιν ἀπὸ τῆς καμίνου προελθόντα τὴν λαμπηδόνα ἀφίησιν.
thought_title: The washing of regeneration remakes, not merely cleanses
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining to the catechumens how baptism's power differs from Jewish purification, arguing that it does not just remove uncleanness but re-creates the whole person.
pass_a_gloss: Do you see that the uncleanness comes not from the nature of the thing, but from the weakness of the reasoning? And again, 'All things are clean, but it is evil for the man who eats with offense.' Do you see that not the eating, but the eating with offense, this is the cause of uncleanness? The Jewish washing cleansed away such a stain; but the washing of grace does not cleanse such a stain, but the uncleanness that truly exists, the stain that has been placed in great measure in the soul along with the body; for it does not make clean those who have touched dead bodies, but those who have touched dead deeds, these it makes clean. Even if someone is soft, even if someone is a fornicator, even if an idolater, even if he has done any terrible thing whatever, even if he has all the wickedness that is among human beings, having fallen into the pool of the waters, he comes up from the divine streams purer than the rays of the sun. And so that you may not think that the things said are boastful talk, hear Paul speaking about the power of the washing: 'Do not be deceived; neither idolaters, nor fornicators, nor adulterers, nor the soft, nor men who lie with males, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will inherit the kingdom of God.' And what does this have to do with the things said, someone says? For the thing sought is to show whether the power of the washing cleanses away all these things. Therefore hear what follows: 'And these things some of you were, but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.' We promise to show you that those who approach the washing become clean from all fornication; but the word demonstrated more, that they become not only clean, but also holy and righteous; for he did not say only 'You were washed,' but also 'You were sanctified and you were justified.' What could be more paradoxical than this, when righteousness is born without toils and sweats and achievements? For such is the love for humanity of the divine gift: without sweats it makes people righteous. For if a letter of a king, a few letters set forth, releases those liable to countless accusations as free men, and leads others also to the greatest honor, much more the Holy Spirit of God, which can do all things, will free us from all wickedness, and will grant us much righteousness, and will fill us with much boldness. And just as a spark falling into the middle of a vast sea would immediately be quenched, or would become invisible, having been drowned by the multitude of the waters; so also all human wickedness, whenever it falls into the pool of the divine streams, is drowned and made to disappear more quickly and more easily than that spark. And for what reason, someone says, if the washing forgives us all our sins, is it not called a washing of forgiveness of sins, nor a washing of cleansing, but a washing of regeneration? Because it does not simply forgive us our sins, nor does it simply cleanse us of our offenses, but in such a way as if we had been born again from above. For it creates us anew from above and fashions us anew, not molding us again from earth, but creating us from another element, the nature of the waters. For it does not simply wipe off the vessel, but it recasts it whole again. For things that are wiped off, even if they are cleansed with precision, have traces of their quality and bear the remains of the stain; but things that have fallen into a smelting furnace and have been renewed through the flame, having put off all filth, when they come forth from the furnace, send forth the same brightness as things newly made.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for baptism as complete re-creation; must be used exactly.
Literal rendering of the vice-list term; keeps the physical metaphor Chrysostom uses without modernizing to a specific sexual category.
Literal gloss of the compound; preserves the source's descriptive force without importing a modern term.
Keeps the double sense of 'from above' and 'again' that Chrysostom exploits in the regeneration argument.
Literal rendering of the metallurgical image; Chrysostom is contrasting wiping with recasting, so the technical term matters.

pass_b_english: Do you see that uncleanness comes not from the nature of the thing itself, but from the weakness of the reasoning? And again: All things are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats to another's stumbling (Romans 14:20). Do you see that it is not the eating, but the eating to another's stumbling, that causes uncleanness?

The Jewish washing cleansed away that kind of stain. But the washing of grace does not cleanse that kind; it cleanses the uncleanness that is truly real, the stain that has been deeply impressed upon the soul along with the body. For it does not make clean those who have touched dead bodies, but those who have touched dead deeds. If a man is soft, if he is a fornicator, if he is an idolater, if he has done anything dreadful at all, if he possesses every wickedness found among human beings—when he falls into the pool of the waters, he comes up from the divine streams purer than the rays of the sun.

And so that you do not think what I am saying is empty boasting, listen to Paul speaking about the power of the washing: Do not be deceived: neither idolaters, nor fornicators, nor adulterers, nor the soft, nor men who lie with males, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:9-10). And what does this have to do with what was said, someone asks? For the question was to show whether the power of the washing cleanses away all these things. Then listen to what follows: And such were some of you, but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:11).

We promised to show you that those who approach the washing become clean from all fornication, but the word has demonstrated something more: that they become not only clean, but also holy and righteous. For he did not say only, You were washed, but also, You were sanctified and justified. What could be more astonishing than this, when righteousness is born without labors and sweat and achievements? Such is the loving-kindness of the divine gift: it makes people righteous without sweat.

If a letter from a king, a few written words set before someone, releases people liable to countless charges and sets them free, and brings others to the greatest honor, how much more will the Holy Spirit of God, who can do all things, deliver us from every evil, grant us abundant righteousness, and fill us with great confidence? And just as a spark falling into the middle of a vast sea would immediately be quenched, or rather would disappear, drowned by the mass of waters, so too all human wickedness, when it falls into the pool of the divine streams, is drowned and destroyed more quickly and easily than that spark.

And why, someone asks, if the washing forgives us all our sins, is it not called a washing of forgiveness of sins, nor a washing of cleansing, but a washing of regeneration? Because it does not simply forgive us our sins, nor simply cleanse us of our offenses, but does so as if we had been born again from above. For it creates us anew and fashions us again, not by molding us from earth, but by creating us from another element, the nature of the waters.

For it does not simply wipe the vessel clean, but recasts it entirely anew. Things that are wiped clean, even if they are cleansed with precision, still bear traces of their former quality and carry the remnants of the stain. But things that fall into a smelting furnace and are renewed through the flame put off all filth and, coming out of the furnace, give off the same brightness as vessels newly made.

problems.why: "Offense" misses the stumbling-block sense; this is about causing another to stumble.

edits.old: but it is evil for the person who eats with offense
edits.new: but it is evil for the person who eats to another's stumbling

edits.old: but the eating with offense, that causes uncleanness
edits.new: but the eating to another's stumbling, that causes uncleanness

fixed: Changed 'with offense' to 'to another's stumbling' in both occurrences, matching διὰ προσκόμματος, which refers to causing another to stumble.

last_rejected.why: "To another's stumbling" misreads διά: it means "through stumbling" not "to another's."
last_rejected.fix: the one who eats with stumbling / the one who eats in a way that causes stumbling
last_rejected.ruling: διὰ προσκόμματος means 'through stumbling'; 'to another's' adds a possessive not in the Greek, but the phrase is idiomatic and meaning is preserved.

last_rejected.why: "Soft" is archaic/unclear for μαλακοὶ (effeminate/passive homosexual partners); obscures Paul's meaning.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Soft' is a literal rendering of μαλακοί within its semantic range; not a major error, just a preference for clarity.

last_rejected.why: ἀρσενοκοῖται are active partners, not just "men who lie with males"; obscures the paired condemnation.
last_rejected.fix: sodomites / those who lie with males
last_rejected.ruling: 'Men who lie with males' is a reasonable rendering of ἀρσενοκοῖται; the active/passive distinction is debated and not clearly wrong.

last_rejected.why: "Robbers" is too narrow; ἅρπαγες means swindlers/exploiters/grabbers, not just thieves.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Robbers' falls within the normal range of ἅρπαγες; a preference for 'swindlers' is not a major error.

last_rejected.why: Repeated: "soft" for μαλακὸς is unclear and archaic; same problem as above.
last_rejected.ruling: Same as #2; 'soft' for μαλακός is within normal range, not a major mistranslation.

last_rejected.why: "Cleansing" for καθάρσεως is flat; this is a technical term for purification/catharsis.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Cleansing' for καθάρσεως is accurate and standard; 'purification' would be a preference, not a correction.
